data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological survival is descriptive/causal; scientific preference is normative/methodological","Organisms do not choose their tests; scientists actively design severe tests","Evolution has no goal of 'truth'; science explicitly aims at verisimilitude"],"overturn_conditions":["If biological fitness could be proven to guarantee future survival, the analogy would support induction, contradicting Popper","If verisimilitude is shown to be unmeasurable even comparatively, the strategic basis for preference vanishes"],"shared_structure":["Selection via elimination of failed candidates","Survival indicates past fitness/test-resistance, not future guarantee","Preference is strategic (choose the strongest to attack/use) not probabilistic"],"source_memory_refs":["popper_conjectures_refutations_ch10","tichy_miller_verisimilitude_1974","darwin_origin_species_ch4"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we bet on the fittest organism to survive the next season without knowing the future, we bet on the best-corroborated theory to solve problems without inductive certainty","The 'cost' in biology is extinction; the 'cost' in Popperian science is the acceptance of radical fallibilism and lack of practical assurance"]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms without smuggling in induction, provided the preference is framed as a methodological rule for maximizing 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) through severe testing rather than an inductive inference of future probability. The cost of accepting this defense is the abandonment of any claim that science converges toward probable truth or offers practical certainty; instead, science becomes a high-risk gamble where the 'best' theory is merely the one currently most worthy of attempted falsification, offering no guarantee of success in application.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd-Miller proof demonstrates that 'verisimilitude' cannot be logically defined for false theories, then the comparison of 'better' vs 'worse' corroborated theories collapses into incoherence.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for the survived theory implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature (that what survived yesterday will survive tomorrow), then the definition of 'induction' used is too narrow and the smuggled premise remains.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists act on theories expecting them to work (practical probability) rather than just to be tested, then Popper's methodological rule fails to describe actual scientific rationality.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument reconstructs Popper's distinction between 'probability' (logical likelihood based on content) and 'corroboration' (historical report of test performance). It posits that preferring a highly corroborated theory is not an inductive leap that it will hold tomorrow, but a rational selection of the theory with the highest surviving 'verisimilitude' content relative to competitors, akin to natural selection where survival indicates fitness against specific pressures but guarantees nothing about future environments. This mechanism treats the preference as a strategic choice to test the strongest available candidate, thereby accelerating error elimination.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
